stem: A RAG scorecard has two halves because…
options: Retrieval (was the right passage found) and generation (what the model did with it) fail separately and one number cannot tell them apart
explanation: hit@k for retrieval; correctness, faithfulness, refusal for generation.

options: Whether any relevant passage is in the top k — in code, no model call, the ceiling on everything else
Identical to production's — an eval measures the system, not a demo of it
explanation: Otherwise the numbers are about nothing.

options: Fast and brittle — the recorded g9 was correct ('one-business-day') and marked wrong by the checker
explanation: Normalise (hyphens, whitespace, numbers) and keep the case.

options: Useful and biased — favours long, confident, well-formatted answers; keep the rubric narrow, use a schema, spot-check by hand
NOT_COVERED exactly when the question is uncovered, and never when it is covered
explanation: Both directions matter: answering uncovered questions is dangerous; refusing covered ones is useless.

stem: hit@3 = 60%, faithfulness = 98%, correctness = 58%. Work first on…
options: Retrieval — the model is faithful to what it gets, but 40% of the time it gets the wrong passages

stem: Faithfulness reads 100% for a month, then hand review finds invented numbers. Lesson?
options: The judge has a blind spot — add code checks (numbers in sources), sharpen the rubric, keep spot-checking
explanation: A too-good number is a prompt to look.

options: A smoke test — real golden sets are hundreds, sampled from traffic and labelled by domain experts
explanation: Scale the set before trusting the numbers (8.2).

stem: A CI gate for RAG should…
options: Run the scorecard on every change to chunking, index, prompt or model, several runs, and block on regression past written thresholds
explanation: Write the thresholds down before you need them.
